transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I just can’t sit still in these meetings or trainings anymore. I feel like I’ve got to get up and move even when everyone else is fine staying put, and it's starting to cause some real trouble for me at work.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'can't sit still' - are you experiencing restlessness, fidgeting, or an inability to remain seated in situations where it's expected of you?

Yes, exactly. In those long safety meetings, my legs start jumping and I get this buzzing feeling under my skin until I just have to stand up and walk around. Even at home or at church, I'm constantly tapping my feet, whispering, or fidgeting because sitting quietly feels almost impossible.
Do you also find it difficult to focus on tasks, follow instructions, or make careless mistakes, in addition to the fidgeting and restlessness you've described?

I haven't really noticed major issues with focusing or making careless mistakes when I'm doing hands-on work. My main struggle is just this constant restlessness, not being able to sit still, and my tendency to jump in too quickly during discussions.

Can you think of any situations where you had to focus on a task that required you to sit still and pay attention, like reading a book or working on a puzzle, and how did you manage in those situations?

Honestly, doing quiet activities like that is almost impossible for me. Even when I'm just trying to watch a game with my wife or sit in church, I'm constantly tapping my feet, fiddling, or whispering because sitting quietly drives me nuts. I can't even sit on the couch for more than a few minutes on my day off without needing to jump up and find something to do.
Can you tell me more about what you mean by 'jumping in too quickly during discussions' - do you often interrupt others, blurt out answers, or have difficulty waiting for your turn to speak?

Yes, it's pretty embarrassing, but during staff briefings I constantly blurt out answers before my supervisor even finishes his question, which often means I misunderstand what he was actually asking. I also get incredibly impatient waiting my turn to talk in meetings, standing in lines, or even playing bingo with my wife, so I end up shifting around, sighing, and just jumping in out of turn.
Can you think of any times when you acted on impulse without much thought, such as spending money, driving recklessly, or quitting a task, and how often does this kind of behavior happen?

I don't really experience those kinds of impulsive behaviors like reckless driving, spending money, or quitting tasks. For me, it's more about getting impatient, blurting out answers, and not being able to sit still rather than doing anything reckless like that.

Can you estimate how often you exhibit these behaviors, such as fidgeting, blurting out answers, or interrupting others, and have you experienced any significant changes in the frequency or severity of these behaviors over time?

These behaviors happen constantly throughout the day, from interrupting in almost every meeting to pacing around the house. While I've had these tendencies since I was a kid in grade school, they became a major problem about a year and a half ago after my promotion. My new supervisor role forces me to sit through long meetings and do desk work rather than staying active on my feet.

You've mentioned that you haven't really noticed major issues with focusing or making careless mistakes, but can you tell me if you have any difficulty with organization, time management, or following through on instructions in your daily life or work?

I don't think I have general problems with organization, time management, or following instructions. The only real issue along those lines is that I struggle to stick with our new scheduling software and have missed some inspection windows. Honestly, I'm not sure if that's a problem with organization or just because of my constant need to get up and move.

Can you think of any situations where you had trouble following through on instructions or had difficulty sustaining attention on tasks that didn't involve physical activity, such as reading, completing paperwork, or listening to someone talk for an extended period?

I definitely struggle with paperwork, safety audits, and listening during long briefings, but it's mostly because of my intense restlessness. During trainings, the urge to get up and move is so strong that I can't focus on what's being said, and I often jump in too fast and misunderstand the instructions. Sitting at a desk to do paperwork or use the scheduling software is just a nightmare because I can't tolerate staying still.

Can you describe how you feel and what you experience when you're engaged in activities that you enjoy and find highly interesting, such as hobbies or sports, and do you still exhibit restlessness or impulsivity in those situations?

Even during things I really enjoy, like watching a game on TV or playing bingo with my wife, I still can't shake the restlessness. When watching a game, I end up tapping my feet, whispering, or fiddling with things because sitting quietly is just too hard. And with bingo, I get so impatient waiting my turn that I'm constantly shifting around, sighing, and sometimes jumping in out of turn.

Can you think of any times when you were able to focus and complete a task without getting distracted or feeling the urge to move, such as a project at work or a personal goal, and how did you manage to stay focused during that time?

Honestly, I can't recall a single time when I was able to sit still and focus on a task without feeling that constant urge to move. I've always had to be active and hands-on to get things done, so sitting quietly to focus has always been a constant struggle for me.
Can you describe a situation where you had to complete a complex task that required sustained mental effort, like a project or a puzzle, and how you managed to stay on track and avoid distractions?

I honestly struggle to think of a time recently where I successfully stayed on track with that kind of task. I usually end up getting completely distracted or just abandoning those projects altogether because sitting still and focusing is so hard for me.
Have you experienced significant symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus during tasks or play activities, in addition to your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity?

I don't really feel like I have trouble focusing or paying attention in that way. My main struggle is just the constant physical restlessness, the overwhelming need to move around, and blurting things out, rather than drifting off or losing focus on tasks.

Can you think of any activities where you were able to sit and focus without feeling restless, such as reading a book, working on a puzzle, or playing a quiet game, and how did you feel during those activities?

There really aren't any quiet activities where I can just sit still and focus. Even during relaxing times like playing bingo, watching a game with my wife, or sitting in church, I get incredibly restless and end up tapping my feet, whispering, or just having to get up and pace. Sitting quietly like that honestly drives me crazy.

Can you tell me if you have more problems with feeling restless and needing to move, or if you have more issues with blurting out answers and interrupting others, and which of these causes you more distress in your daily life?

Both are major issues for me, but they show up in different ways; I get this buzzing feeling under my skin and jumping legs where I just *have* to get up, but I also constantly cut people off and blurt out answers in briefings. While blurting things out causes immediate embarrassment and trouble with my boss, it's the constant physical restlessness and inability to sit still that truly drives me crazy and pushed me to seek help, since it's hurting both my job and my marriage.

Can you think of any situations where you were able to engage in a quiet, mentally demanding task, like solving a crossword puzzle or studying, without feeling the urge to move or getting distracted, and how did you manage to stay focused during that time?

I honestly can't think of a single time I've been able to do a quiet, mentally demanding task like that without feeling a constant urge to move. Even during quiet times at home, like trying to watch a game or just sit still, I always end up fidgeting, tapping my feet, and needing to get up after just a few minutes.

Can you estimate the frequency of days when you experienced significant symptoms of hyperactivity, such as fidgeting or restlessness, versus days when you had significant symptoms of impulsivity, like blurting out answers or interrupting others, over the past month?

I haven't really tracked the exact number of days or kept a tally of which symptom happens on which day. But honestly, both the restlessness and the interrupting feel like they happen pretty much every single day, especially when I am at work.
Can you describe any situations where you were able to complete a task that required sustained mental effort without getting distracted, and how did you manage to stay on track?

I really can't think of any situations where I successfully managed sustained mental effort without getting restless or distracted. Desk work, paperwork, and long tasks have always been a major struggle for me, especially since my promotion. I honestly don't have any tricks or coping mechanisms that work for staying on track.

Can you compare the distress or impairment you experience from your physical restlessness and need to move versus the distress or impairment from blurting out answers and interrupting others, and which one do you feel is more problematic in your daily life?

The physical restlessness is a constant, exhausting struggle—I feel like a wind-up toy that can't stop pacing, which makes me leave meetings and causes arguments with my wife at church or bingo. On the other hand, blurting out answers in briefings directly damages my professional standing because I constantly misunderstand my supervisor and look bad. While the restlessness is a more constant daily battle, the interrupting has definitely had the most immediate, negative impact on my job security.

Do you think your main issue is more with controlling your physical movements and restlessness, or with controlling your impulses and blurting out answers, and which one do you feel is causing you more problems in your daily life?

Both are huge struggles, but the physical restlessness—like the constant buzzing under my skin and needing to pace—is an exhausting daily battle at work and at home with my wife. However, the impulsiveness of blurting out answers and cutting people off in briefings is what has really landed me in hot water professionally, leading to me misunderstanding instructions and getting written up.
Do you feel that your difficulties with restlessness and fidgeting are more prominent than your issues with blurting out answers and interrupting others, or are they equally problematic for you?

I'm honestly not quite sure which one is worse, because both of them cause me major, distinct problems. The physical restlessness is a constant, exhausting battle at home and during meetings, but my tendency to interrupt and blurt things out is what's really putting my job security in danger.
Have you experienced any symptoms of hyperactivity or restlessness in childhood, or did these symptoms develop later in life, perhaps around the time of your promotion?

They definitely go back to childhood—my mom still talks about how my grade school teachers called her because I couldn't stay in my seat, blurted out answers, and wandered the classroom. I've always been this way, but it only became a major problem about a year and a half ago after my promotion. That's when I suddenly had to sit through long meetings and do desk work, which made these symptoms start impacting my job.

Can you tell me if you have experienced significant symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus during tasks, in addition to your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, and how do they compare in terms of frequency and impact on your daily life?

I don't really experience traditional inattention or having my mind drift off. My main struggle is the intense physical restlessness and impatience, like the constant need to move or jumping in too quickly. It's not that I can't focus on the work itself, it's just that sitting still to do it is almost impossible.
Can you think of any tasks where you had to focus and had trouble because your mind wandered or you had difficulty following through, rather than because you couldn't sit still?

No, I really can't think of any times where my mind just wandered off on its own. My struggle is always the intense physical restlessness and the urge to move or speak out of turn, rather than my brain drifting off or losing focus.

Can you estimate the relative frequency or severity of your hyperactive symptoms, such as restlessness and fidgeting, compared to your impulsive symptoms, like blurting out answers and interrupting others, to help clarify which might be more predominant?

I'm not quite sure which one is worse or happens more frequently, as both the physical restlessness and the tendency to blurt things out feel very constant and disruptive to me. They both just seem to happen all the time, and I haven't really tried to compare them. It just feels like one big, ongoing struggle every day.

Do you think your symptoms of restlessness and fidgeting are more bothersome to you and cause more problems in your daily life than your symptoms of blurting out answers and interrupting others, or are they equally problematic?

They really feel almost equally problematic to me, just in different ways. The physical restlessness and constant pacing are exhausting and make it impossible to sit through church or meetings, but the blurting out and interrupting is what directly gets me into trouble with my boss and my wife. It's frustrating because they both just feed into each other.

Can you recall any instances where you were able to engage in a quiet activity, like reading or working on a puzzle, without feeling restless, and were you able to complete it without getting distracted?

I really can't recall any times where I could do a quiet activity without feeling restless. Even simple things like sitting on the couch on my day off, watching a game with my wife, or sitting in church drive me nuts. I always end up tapping my feet, fiddling, or just getting up after a couple of minutes because I can't stand sitting still.

Can you compare how much your restlessness and fidgeting versus your impulsivity and blurting out answers have impacted your work and personal relationships, and which one do you feel has caused more significant problems for you?

My physical restlessness causes constant arguments with my wife because I can't sit through church or bingo, and it annoys my boss when I keep getting up during meetings. Meanwhile, my impulsivity and blurting out answers have directly damaged my job performance, leading to misunderstood instructions, a messed-up scheduling system, and a write-up. While the restlessness is an exhausting daily physical struggle, the jumping in out of turn has definitely caused more immediate trouble for my job security.

Can you tell me if you experience more distress or impairment from your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus, or if it's mainly the hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms that cause you problems, and which ones do you think are more prominent?

It is definitely the hyperactivity and impulsivity that cause almost all of my distress and problems. My struggle isn't that my mind drifts off or that I'm daydreaming, but rather this intense physical need to move, not being able to sit in meetings, and my habit of blurting things out. Those physical urges and impulsive behaviors are what are causing all the trouble at my job and with my wife.

Do you think your symptoms of hyperactivity, such as restlessness and fidgeting, are more prominent and cause more problems in your daily life than your symptoms of impulsivity, such as blurting out answers and interrupting others, or are they equally problematic?

They really feel almost equally disruptive, just in different ways. The physical restlessness and inability to sit still constantly drive me out of meetings and make church or relaxing at home impossible, while the blurting out and interrupting cause me to misunderstand work instructions and argue with my wife. It’s incredibly frustrating because both of these things are actively threatening my job security and my marriage right now.
